title: Feds launch recruitment for independent Miscarriage of Justice Review Commission
summary: Guilt or innocence will not be determined by the commission, but it will instead investigate potential miscarriage of justice and may order a remedy, such as a new trial or new appeal.

image.caption: Canadian Justice Minister and Attorney General of Canada Sean Fraser announced Monday that the federal government will begin recruitment of commissioners for the independent Miscarriage of Justice Review Commission. (Adrian Wyld/The Canadian Press)

blocks.text: Guilt or innocence will not be determined by the commission, but it will instead investigate potential miscarriage of justice and may order a remedy, such as a new trial or new appeal.
Current criminal conviction review process was last reformed in 2002
The Canadian government is launching its recruitment for the independent Miscarriage of Justice Review Commission, the federal justice department announced Monday in a press release.

"Wrongful convictions can have lasting consequences. We’re taking the next step in establishing a commission that will review these cases independently of government," Justice Minister and Attorney General of Canada Sean Fraser said in the release.
The Winnipeg-based commission will operate at arm's length from government and independently of police, prosecutors and the courts.

Guilt or innocence will not be determined by the commission, but it will instead investigate potential miscarriage of justice and may order a remedy, such as a new trial or new appeal, the release said.

Since 1892, the justice minister has had the authority under the Criminal Code to order a new trial or appeal when new evidence shows a miscarriage of justice likely occurred. This will continue until the commission opens.

The current criminal conviction review process was last reformed in 2002, and since then 236 completed applications were received, with the justice minister having made decisions on remedies for 36 individuals.
Of those 36 decisions, 16 were made in the last five years. In total, the justice minister has ordered 16 new trials and 18 new appeals, and rejected 2 applications, according to the release.
"Our responsibility is to make sure Canadians can trust their justice system, and that means, in rare cases, returning cases to court to consider new information," Fraser said in the release.
Former Winnipegger David Milgaard was 16 years old when he was wrongfully convicted of killing Saskatoon nursing aide Gail Miller. He spent 23 years behind bars trying to prove his innocence. (CBC)

The Liberal government introduced legislation in 2023 to create an independent commission that would be tasked with reviewing miscarriage of justice claims. The Miscarriage of Justice Review Commission Act, also known as David and Joyce Milgaard's Law, was passed in December 2024.

The late David Milgaard, who was from Winnipeg, was 16 at the time of Saskatoon nursing aide Gail Miller's murder in 1969. He spent 23 years in prison for a crime he did not commit, with both the Saskatchewan Court of Appeal and the Supreme Court of Canada both refusing to hear Milgaard's appeal in 1971.
After his release and exoneration, Milgaard spent his life advocating for the wrongfully convicted.

blocks.text: The establishment of the commission is in response to calls from stakeholders and advocates for the wrongly convicted and follows the establishment of similar independent commissions in other countries, including England, Scotland and New Zealand, the release said.
"I'm just having good faith that it's going to be the right people and it's going to be done as soon as humanly possible," Milgaard's sister Susan Milgaard told CBC in 2025.
"Because every single day that you and I have here is another wrongfully convicted person sitting there, still locked up."
